newsitem.title: MALI: Tuareg peace boosts Mali tourism.
newsitem.headline: Tuareg peace boosts Mali tourism.

text.p: Tourist arrivals in the West African state of Mali, which includes the ancient city of Timbuktu amongst its attractions, have revived following a 1995 peace agreement with Tuareg rebels, officials say.
Tourist commissioner Aguibou Guisse told Reuters that the number of arrivals rose to 60,000 in 1996 having slumped to just over 30,000 in 1993.
The annual total before the Tuareg took up arms in 1990 was around 44,000 although this topped 50,000 before the conflict really took hold.

"Today it's very difficult to find an available room in the hotels in Bamako or the other tourist regions such as Mopti and Timbuktu," Guisse said, noting that privatisation and restructuring had also helped stimulate the sector.

He said that the peace deal meant that the sector could revive a plan to invest 21.4 billion CFA francs ($37.5 million) between 1990 and 2005. "It's a question of promoting all aspects of the sector -- layout of sites, places to stay, airfields, road, telecommunications, banks," he said.
Mali's main foreign exchange earners are cotton, gold and livestock.

Official figures showed that the number of hotels rose from 67 in 1993 to 86 in 1996 while the number of rooms rose from 1,164 to 1,582 between 1990 and 1995. The number of travel agencies has risen from from five to about 20 in three years.
The Tuaregs, light-skinned nomads of Moorish descent, took up arms in Mali and Niger in 1990 complaining of domination by black-majority governments.
